variants.title: Measure the whole serving path
variants.context: A quantized candidate is measured on the whole serving path in four steps: freeze the comparison, inspect execution, measure deployment, then re-evaluate behavior. A smaller artifact is a claim about bytes, not about latency.
variants.prompt: An INT8 candidate is ready for benchmarking against the FP32 baseline. Put the measurement steps in order.

items.text: Inspect execution: confirm every required operator uses the intended path and record fallbacks, casts, and transfer boundaries.
Freeze the comparison: use identical preprocessing, requests, batch shapes, concurrency, warmup, and runtime versions.
Measure deployment: compare artifact bytes, peak memory, cold start, sustained throughput, and latency percentiles on the target device.
Re-evaluate behavior: run aggregate metrics, calibration, downstream thresholds, and important slices against the higher-precision artifact.

variants.hint: One step decides whether the numbers you are about to collect describe the intended graph at all.
variants.explanation: Execution coverage is checked before performance is believed, because a silent fallback produces real numbers for the wrong graph.

variants.title: Measure the whole serving path
variants.context: A quantized candidate is measured on the whole serving path in four steps: freeze the comparison, inspect execution, measure deployment, then re-evaluate behavior. A smaller artifact is a claim about bytes, not about latency.
variants.prompt: A reviewer asks why the reported 4x size win did not reduce cost. Put the steps in order to produce an answer.

items.text: Re-evaluate behavior: confirm the quality slices still hold so the finding is about performance and not a broken artifact.
Measure deployment: report latency percentiles, peak memory, and throughput rather than the weight-storage ratio.
Freeze the comparison: rebuild both runs under one preprocessing, request mix, batch shape, and runtime version.
Inspect execution: read the compiled graph to find which nodes ran at higher precision and where conversions were inserted.

variants.hint: The size ratio and the cost question are answered by different measurements.
variants.explanation: Bit-width reduction is a storage ratio, so cost claims require measured latency, memory, and throughput on the target hardware.

variants.title: Measure the whole serving path
variants.context: A quantized candidate is measured on the whole serving path in four steps: freeze the comparison, inspect execution, measure deployment, then re-evaluate behavior. A smaller artifact is a claim about bytes, not about latency.
variants.prompt: The target fleet is moving from one accelerator generation to the next. Put the steps in order for the re-measurement.

items.text: Re-evaluate behavior: rerun the quality slices, because a different kernel can change accumulation and numeric behavior.
Freeze the comparison: pin the new driver, runtime, and kernel versions for both the baseline and the candidate.
Inspect execution: recheck operator coverage, since supported kernels and granularities change with the device generation.
Measure deployment: collect artifact bytes, peak memory, cold start, throughput, and percentiles on the new hardware.

variants.hint: Support is the intersection of format, granularity, operator, runtime, and device.
variants.explanation: A precision choice is not permanent, so every hardware or runtime change reopens both the coverage and the performance evidence.

variants.title: Release with a rollback path
variants.context: Promotion is staged so a numeric change stays reversible: shadow first where outputs can be compared, canary on the same device class and traffic mix, monitor fallbacks and drift, and keep the higher-precision artifact loadable throughout.
variants.prompt: The INT8 candidate has cleared its gates and is ready for traffic. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Hold the higher-precision artifact loadable under the same request contract until promotion completes.
Shadow the candidate so its outputs can be compared against production without affecting users.
Monitor runtime errors, fallback counts, latency distribution, memory pressure, and output drift.
Canary on the same device class, runtime, input shapes, and traffic mix used by the benchmark.

variants.hint: Comparison without user impact comes before comparison with it.
variants.explanation: Staged exposure keeps the numeric change reversible, because the rollback artifact must stay loadable under the same contract.

variants.title: Release with a rollback path
variants.context: Promotion is staged so a numeric change stays reversible: shadow first where outputs can be compared, canary on the same device class and traffic mix, monitor fallbacks and drift, and keep the higher-precision artifact loadable throughout.
variants.prompt: During canary, fallback counts rise and p99 latency drifts above the envelope. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Invalidate any cache or warmed state that was populated by the candidate's outputs.
Stop promotion under the predeclared trigger so no further traffic reaches the candidate.
Reopen the evidence with both artifact manifests so the numeric and execution plans can be compared.
Return traffic to the higher-precision artifact, which is still loadable under the same request contract.

variants.hint: The first move protects users, not the investigation.
variants.explanation: A rehearsed rollback names who can stop promotion, how fast traffic returns, and which state must be invalidated before analysis begins.

variants.title: Release with a rollback path
variants.context: Promotion is staged so a numeric change stays reversible: shadow first where outputs can be compared, canary on the same device class and traffic mix, monitor fallbacks and drift, and keep the higher-precision artifact loadable throughout.
variants.prompt: A quantized model changes the score threshold a downstream service uses. Put the steps in order for a safe rollout.

items.text: Monitor output drift and the named quality proxies rather than only latency and memory.
Confirm that switching model files alone restores the previous system before calling the rollback compatible.
Shadow both artifacts so the threshold shift can be measured on real traffic before anyone depends on it.
Canary with the downstream threshold pinned to the artifact version that produced it.

variants.hint: Ask what else would have to change back for a rollback to actually work.
variants.explanation: Rollback compatibility is part of the artifact contract, so a candidate that moves thresholds or schemas is not reversible by file swap alone.

variants.title: Map a value into the INT8 grid
variants.context: Uniform affine INT8 quantization maps real values onto codes from -128 to 127, which is 255 steps. scale = (real_max - real_min) / 255, zero_point = round(-128 - real_min / scale), and code = round(real / scale) + zero_point.
variants.prompt: Calibration observes activations in the range -3.6 to 1.5. Using asymmetric INT8, what integer code represents the real value 1.0?
variants.hint: Compute the step size first, then the code that stands for real zero.
variants.explanation: The scale is 5.1 over 255, which is 0.02, the zero point is 52, and 1.0 divided by 0.02 plus 52 gives code 102.

mistakes.feedback: That is the scaled value without the zero point, so real zero would not land on the right code.
That uses -128 as the zero point instead of deriving it from the observed minimum.

variants.title: Map a value into the INT8 grid
variants.context: Uniform affine INT8 quantization maps real values onto codes from -128 to 127, which is 255 steps. scale = (real_max - real_min) / 255, zero_point = round(-128 - real_min / scale), and code = round(real / scale) + zero_point.
variants.prompt: A tighter clipping policy gives the range -1.05 to 1.50. Using asymmetric INT8, what integer code represents the real value 0.5?
variants.hint: A narrower range makes the step finer, which changes both terms of the mapping.
variants.explanation: The scale is 2.55 over 255, which is 0.01, the zero point is -23, and 0.5 divided by 0.01 plus -23 gives code 27.

mistakes.feedback: That drops the zero point, which is what shifts an asymmetric range onto the signed grid.
That subtracts the negative zero point instead of adding it, moving the code the wrong way.

variants.title: Map a value into the INT8 grid
variants.context: Uniform affine INT8 quantization maps real values onto codes from -128 to 127, which is 255 steps. scale = (real_max - real_min) / 255, zero_point = round(-128 - real_min / scale), and code = round(real / scale) + zero_point.
variants.prompt: A wider corpus pushes the observed range to -15.3 to 10.2. Using asymmetric INT8, what integer code represents the real value 4.0?
variants.hint: A wider range means a coarser step before anything else changes.
variants.explanation: The scale is 25.5 over 255, which is 0.1, the zero point is 25, and 4.0 divided by 0.1 plus 25 gives code 65.

mistakes.feedback: That is the scaled value with no zero point, so the mapping no longer represents real zero exactly.
That subtracts the zero point instead of adding it, which mirrors the value around zero.

variants.title: Diagnose the quantized candidate
variants.context: Quantization benefits must be measured on the actual model, runtime, operator graph, batch shape, and device. Unsupported operators can execute at higher precision silently, and a calibration corpus decides which real values are representable.
variants.prompt: An INT8 artifact is one quarter the size of the FP32 baseline, but p95 latency is unchanged. A runtime trace shows two matrix multiplications running in higher precision with conversions inserted around them. What is the finding?
options: Unsupported operators fell back, so conversion overhead cancels the traffic saved by the quantized weights.
The batch shape is too small to amortize kernel launch cost, so the same graph will be faster at higher concurrency.
The device needs a longer warmup before quantized kernels reach their steady-state clock and cache behavior.
optionFeedback: Correct: silent fallback keeps the outputs correct while erasing the latency benefit and adding conversion work.
Concurrency can change throughput, but it does not explain nodes executing at a precision the plan did not choose.
Warmup affects early requests, while the trace shows a persistent execution path rather than a startup effect.
variants.hint: Read the execution plan, not the file size.
variants.explanation: An artifact can hold low-precision weights while unsupported operations execute at higher precision, so operator coverage is inspected on the target rather than inferred from a successful export.

variants.title: Diagnose the quantized candidate
variants.context: Quantization benefits must be measured on the actual model, runtime, operator graph, batch shape, and device. Unsupported operators can execute at higher precision silently, and a calibration corpus decides which real values are representable.
variants.prompt: Calibration ran on typical inputs with an observed maximum of 4.4, but production activations reach 12.4 on a rare glare slice. That slice degrades badly after conversion. What is the correct fix?
options: Exclude the glare slice from the evaluation set, since it falls outside the distribution the model was calibrated for.
Rebuild the calibration corpus so it includes the rare glare slice, then recompute the ranges and re-evaluate.
Widen the clipping policy to the full observed calibration range, which keeps every calibration value representable.
optionFeedback: Removing the slice from evaluation hides a production failure instead of measuring or fixing it.
Correct: calibration data chooses the representable range, so a corpus missing a real slice guarantees clamping on it.
Widening within the same corpus still stops at 4.4, because the corpus never contained the values being clipped.
variants.hint: Ask which values the corpus ever showed the observer.
variants.explanation: Calibration examples must follow the real input contract and cover rare high-magnitude cases, because values outside the chosen range are clamped to an endpoint.

variants.title: Diagnose the quantized candidate
variants.context: Quantization benefits must be measured on the actual model, runtime, operator graph, batch shape, and device. Unsupported operators can execute at higher precision silently, and a calibration corpus decides which real values are representable.
variants.prompt: A candidate cleared its latency and size gates, but the benchmark ran on a newer accelerator with a different runtime build than the production fleet. What should the gate do?
options: Accept the latency evidence and rerun only the quality slices, which do not depend on the accelerator.
Treat the target-device evidence as missing and rerun the benchmark on the production hardware and runtime.
Accept the result and apply a conservative margin, since the production fleet is older and therefore slower.
optionFeedback: Numeric behavior can change with accumulation and kernel choice, so quality is not device-independent either.
Correct: comparing across devices or runtimes measures a different system, so the required evidence has not been produced.
A margin invented after the fact is not a measurement, and kernel support can differ rather than only speed.
variants.hint: Which configuration will actually serve production traffic?
variants.explanation: A release gate fails closed on unmeasured target hardware, because operator support, kernels, and numeric behavior all vary with device and runtime.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Quantization design is made of parts with distinct jobs. Granularity decides who shares a scale, the workflow decides when parameters are computed, and the manifest decides what makes two artifacts named int8 actually comparable.
variants.prompt: Match each quantization granularity to what it trades.

pairs.label: Per tensor
pairs.detail: One scale and zero point for everything, with small metadata but a coarse step when one channel is large.

pairs.label: Per channel
pairs.detail: One parameter set per output channel, representing differently scaled channels at the cost of extra metadata.

pairs.label: Per group or block
pairs.detail: Small groups share parameters, trading metadata and kernel complexity against local range fidelity.

variants.hint: Ask who is forced to share a step size with whom.
variants.explanation: Granularity decides which values share a scale, and the runtime contract decides which of those choices a kernel can actually execute.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Quantization design is made of parts with distinct jobs. Granularity decides who shares a scale, the workflow decides when parameters are computed, and the manifest decides what makes two artifacts named int8 actually comparable.
variants.prompt: Match each quantization workflow to when its parameters are computed.

pairs.label: Static PTQ
pairs.detail: Representative calibration inputs fix activation parameters before the trained model is converted.

pairs.label: Dynamic activation
pairs.detail: Weights are stored at lower precision and activation ranges are derived per input at runtime.

pairs.label: QAT
pairs.detail: Fake quantization runs during training so parameters can adapt to rounding and clipping error.

variants.hint: Ask when the activation range is known: before the run, during it, or during training.
variants.explanation: PTQ is the first experiment when calibration is representative and the operators are supported, and escalation happens only after diagnostics say where it failed.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: Quantization design is made of parts with distinct jobs. Granularity decides who shares a scale, the workflow decides when parameters are computed, and the manifest decides what makes two artifacts named int8 actually comparable.
variants.prompt: Match each artifact manifest field to what it makes reproducible.

pairs.label: Format and granularity
pairs.detail: The numeric mapping, so two artifacts named int8 are not assumed equivalent.

pairs.label: Calibration manifest
pairs.detail: Which examples chose the representable range and which slices they covered.

pairs.label: Runtime and device identifiers
pairs.detail: The execution plan that produced the benchmark, including exporter, compiler, and driver.

pairs.label: Rollback checksum
pairs.detail: The higher-precision artifact that must stay loadable under the same request contract.

variants.hint: Ask what a reviewer would have to guess if the field were missing.
variants.explanation: The manifest is what keeps two similarly named artifacts from being compared as if their numeric and runtime contracts matched.
